draft.title: Communication and dominance matrices
card: Communication matrix
A binary matrix where 1 means the row person can send a message directly to the column person, and 0 means they cannot. A message may go one way only.
Dominance matrix
A binary matrix where 1 means the row player beat the column player. Each pair plays once, so a 1 in one place means a 0 in the matching place across the diagonal.
Row sums count direct links or wins. The matrix squared, M², counts two-step links: the entry in row i and column j is the number of ways to go from i to j through one other person.
M + M² counts all one-step and two-step links. Example: if A beat B and B beat C, then A has 1 direct win and 1 two-step win over C. Ranking uses row sums of M + M².
draft.remember: Row sums of M count direct links. Row sums of M + M² count direct and two-step links.

a.q: In a dominance matrix, the row sums of M are P: 2, Q: 1, R: 1, S: 0. Which player has the most direct wins?
a.why: Each row sum counts the direct wins of that player, so the largest row sum is P with 2. S has the smallest row sum, so S has no direct wins, not the most.
a.clue: A row sum counts the 1s in that player's row.

b.q: Messages in a team are shown by this communication matrix, with rows and columns in the order A, B, C: row A is 0 1 1, row B is 0 0 1, row C is 1 0 0. How many two-step ways are there to send a message from A to C?
b.why: A two-step path from A to C goes through B or C. A to B then B to C works. A to C then C to C does not, as C has a 0 for C to C. So there is 1 way. Counting the direct link A to C as well would give 2, but that is a one-step link.
b.clue: Check each middle person: can A reach them, and can they reach C?

problems.detail: The example 'A has 1 direct win and 1 two-step win over C' can be read as A having a direct win over C. In fact the direct win is over B and only the two-step win is over C. Say this clearly, e.g. '1 direct win (over B) and 1 two-step win (over C)'.
The stem gives the row sums directly, so the student only has to pick the largest number from a list. This is far too easy for Year 12 and does not test reading a dominance matrix.

check.summary: Both answers check out: P has the most direct wins, and there is 1 two-step path from A to C. The card's example of a two-step win is worded ambiguously, and question a is too easy because it hands the student the row sums.
